claim: Bacillus subtilis ParB forms multimeric networks involving non-specific DNA binding leading to DNA condensation.
source: Bacillus subtilis ParB forms multimeric networks involving non-specific DNA binding leading to DNA condensation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of ParB.

claim: An excess of the free C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB impeded DNA condensation or promoted decondensation of pre-assembled networks.
source: Previously, we found that an excess of the free C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB impeded DNA condensation or promoted decondensation of pre-assembled networks (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: At non-permissive forces for condensation, ParB binds non-specifically and highly dynamically to DNA.
source: At non-permissive forces for condensation, ParB binds non-specifically and highly dynamically to DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The free CTD blocks the formation of ParB networks by heterodimerisation with full length DNA-bound ParB.
source: Our new approach concluded that the free CTD blocks the formation of ParB networks by heterodimerisation with full length DNA-bound ParB.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The CTD acts as a key bridging interface between distal DNA binding loci within ParB networks.
source: This strongly supports a model in which the CTD acts as a key bridging interface between distal DNA binding loci within ParB networks.
evidence: This is a model interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Type I partition systems include an ATPase motor protein ParA, a DNA binding protein ParB, and a centromere-like DNA sequence parS.
source: Type I partition systems, also known as ParABS include an ATPase motor protein, ParA, responsible for the movement of the replicated chromosomes to the distal pole of the cell, a DNA binding protein ParB, and a centromere-like DNA sequence, parS (Funnell, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Funnell, 2016.

claim: ParA is responsible for the movement of the replicated chromosomes to the distal pole of the cell.
source: Type I partition systems, also known as ParABS include an ATPase motor protein, ParA, responsible for the movement of the replicated chromosomes to the distal pole of the cell, a DNA binding protein ParB, and a centromere-like DNA sequence, parS (Funnell, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Funnell, 2016.

claim: Type I partition systems have been described in many bacteria, including Bacillus subtilis.
source: This type of partition system has been described in many bacteria, including Bacillus subtilis, where it is involved in chromosome segregation and sporulation (Mierzejewska and Jagura-Burdzy, 2012) (Yamaichi and Niki, 2000) (Sharpe and Errington, 1996) (Lin and Grossman, 1998) (Lee and Grossman, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, the partition system is involved in chromosome segregation and sporulation.
source: This type of partition system has been described in many bacteria, including Bacillus subtilis, where it is involved in chromosome segregation and sporulation (Mierzejewska and Jagura-Burdzy, 2012) (Yamaichi and Niki, 2000) (Sharpe and Errington, 1996) (Lin and Grossman, 1998) (Lee and Grossman, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: B. subtilis Structural Maintenance of Chromosome (SMC) proteins are loaded by ParB at parS sites in vivo.
source: Importantly, the discovery that B. subtilis Structural Maintenance of Chromosome (SMC) proteins are loaded by ParB at parS sites in vivo and that parS sites act as condensation centers highlights the critical role played by ParB in chromosome organisation (Gruber and Errington, 2009) (Sullivan et al., 2009) (Umbarger et al., 2011) (Broedersz et al., 2014) (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: parS sites act as condensation centers.
source: Importantly, the discovery that B. subtilis Structural Maintenance of Chromosome (SMC) proteins are loaded by ParB at parS sites in vivo and that parS sites act as condensation centers highlights the critical role played by ParB in chromosome organisation (Gruber and Errington, 2009) (Sullivan et al., 2009) (Umbarger et al., 2011) (Broedersz et al., 2014) (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: ParB plays a critical role in chromosome organisation.
source: Importantly, the discovery that B. subtilis Structural Maintenance of Chromosome (SMC) proteins are loaded by ParB at parS sites in vivo and that parS sites act as condensation centers highlights the critical role played by ParB in chromosome organisation (Gruber and Errington, 2009) (Sullivan et al., 2009) (Umbarger et al., 2011) (Broedersz et al., 2014) (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: ParB proteins can bind non-specifically to DNA, spreading several kilobases around parS sites.
source: Interestingly, apart from the specific binding to partition sites, ParB proteins can also bind non-specifically to DNAs spreading several kilobases around parS sites (Breier and Grossman, 2007) (Murray et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ParB spreading is achieved by a limited number of ParB protomers.
source: This spreading is achieved by a limited number of ParB protomers, which has been rationalised by models of ParB-mediated bridging and condensation of DNA supported by in vitro analysis (Graham et al., 2014) (Taylor et al., 2015) (Fisher et al., 2017) (Broedersz et al., 2014) (Sanchez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The generation of ParB networks in vivo requires the presence of specific and non-specific DNA-binding domains in ParB as well as multimerisation interfaces between ParB proteins.
source: The generation of these 'ParB networks' in vivo necessarily requires the presence of specific and non-specific DNA-binding domains in ParB as well as multimerisation interfaces between ParB proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of ParB networks.

claim: Both the N- and C-terminal domains are implicated in forming and maintaining bridging interactions in ParB networks.
source: Recent work has begun to unpick the structural basis for formation of these networks and has implicated both the N- and C-terminal domains in forming and maintaining bridging interactions (Leonard et al., 2004) (Fisher et al., 2017) (Song et al., 2017) (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The CTD of ParB has a dimeric stoichiometry.
source: In our previous work (Fisher et al., 2017), we studied the role of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB in its multimerisation and DNA condensation. In particular, we confirmed its dimeric stoichiometry and identified a novel intermolecular non-specific DNA-binding site across the positively-charged β-sheet face of the CTD of ParB, which was critical for DNA condensation.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: A novel intermolecular non-specific DNA-binding site exists across the positively-charged β-sheet face of the CTD of ParB.
source: In our previous work (Fisher et al., 2017), we studied the role of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB in its multimerisation and DNA condensation. In particular, we confirmed its dimeric stoichiometry and identified a novel intermolecular non-specific DNA-binding site across the positively-charged β-sheet face of the CTD of ParB, which was critical for DNA condensation.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: The non-specific DNA-binding site on the CTD is critical for DNA condensation.
source: In our previous work (Fisher et al., 2017), we studied the role of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of ParB in its multimerisation and DNA condensation. In particular, we confirmed its dimeric stoichiometry and identified a novel intermolecular non-specific DNA-binding site across the positively-charged β-sheet face of the CTD of ParB, which was critical for DNA condensation.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of an excess of the CTD prevented DNA condensation by ParB in vitro and in vivo.
source: We also showed that the presence of an excess of the CTD prevented DNA condensation by ParB and induced disruption of ParB networks in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: The presence of an excess of the CTD induced disruption of ParB networks in vitro and in vivo.
source: We also showed that the presence of an excess of the CTD prevented DNA condensation by ParB and induced disruption of ParB networks in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: CTD variants defective for DNA binding are unlikely to mediate ParB-network disruption by direct competition for DNA binding sites.
source: Our previous experiments with CTD variants defective for DNA binding suggested that ParB-network disruption was unlikely to be mediated by direct competition for DNA binding sites (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: ParB binding and DNA condensation signals were tightly coupled in previous experiments.
source: However, because the ParB binding and DNA condensation signals were tightly coupled (Taylor et al., 2015) (Fisher et al., 2017), it was not possible to separate ParB binding from condensation or to correlate both measurements in parallel.
evidence: This is a limitation of previous work cited from Taylor et al., 2015 and Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: The capping model uniquely predicts that the free CTD will inhibit DNA condensation but not DNA binding.
source: This precluded a direct test of our favoured capping model, which predicts (uniquely) that the free CTD will inhibit DNA condensation but not DNA binding.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed capping model.

claim: In ensemble experiments using electrophoretic mobility shift assays and ParB-protein-induced fluorescence enhancement assays, the signal reported is concomitant to protein binding and condensation.
source: For instance, in ensemble experiments using electrophoretic mobility shift assays and ParB-protein-induced fluorescence enhancement assays, the signal reported is concomitant to protein binding and condensation (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation of ensemble experiments cited from Taylor et al., 2015.

claim: In single-molecule stretch-flow fluorescence experiments, condensation-deficient mutants are required to determine the kinetic parameters of DNA binding.
source: The same happens in single-molecule stretch-flow fluorescence experiments (Graham et al., 2014) requiring the use of condensation-deficient mutants to determine the kinetic parameters of DNA binding (Song and Loparo, 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation of stretch-flow experiments cited from Graham et al., 2014 and Song and Loparo, 2015.

claim: In stretch-flow experiments, condensation is restricted to the free end of the molecule due to a decreasing force gradient along the DNA.
source: Additionally, in stretch-flow experiments, condensation is restricted to the free end of the molecule due to a decreasing force gradient along the DNA.
evidence: This is a limitation of stretch-flow experiments based on the physics of the technique.

claim: Magnetic Tweezers experiments can apply uniform force and can be used to prevent DNA condensation.
source: Magnetic Tweezers (MT) experiments overcome some of these difficulties in that the applied force is uniform and can be used to prevent DNA condensation.
evidence: This is a known property of Magnetic Tweezers technique.

claim: In Magnetic Tweezers, it is possible to measure DNA condensation when the force is decreased to permissive levels.
source: It is therefore possible to measure DNA condensation when the force is decreased to permissive levels (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a capability of Magnetic Tweezers cited from Taylor et al., 2015.

claim: In conventional Magnetic Tweezers, it is not possible to visualise and determine the degree of protein binding to DNA molecules.
source: Nonetheless, in MT it is not possible to visualise and determine the degree of protein binding to DNA molecules.
evidence: This is a limitation of conventional Magnetic Tweezers.

claim: The combination of lateral MT with TIRF microscopy allows simultaneous control of force applied to DNA and visualization of ParB proteins by fluorescence.
source: Here, we have combined lateral MT with total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy (Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2018) to simultaneously control the force applied to DNA and to visualise ParB proteins by fluorescence.
evidence: This is a methodological capability of the combined technique developed in this work.

claim: The combination of MT-TIRF with multilaminar flow technology facilitates rapid exposure of DNA to different protein concentrations.
source: In addition, the combination of our MT-TIRF device with multilaminar flow technology facilitated the rapid exposure of DNA to different protein concentrations and provided a method to precisely capture the kinetics of binding and unbinding events.
evidence: This is a methodological capability of the combined technique developed in this work.

claim: The MT-TIRF device with multilaminar flow provides a method to precisely capture the kinetics of binding and unbinding events.
source: In addition, the combination of our MT-TIRF device with multilaminar flow technology facilitated the rapid exposure of DNA to different protein concentrations and provided a method to precisely capture the kinetics of binding and unbinding events.
evidence: This is a methodological capability of the combined technique developed in this work.

claim: The inhibition of ParB condensation by the free CTD occurs without displacement of full length ParB from DNA.
source: The experimental platform used here allowed us to confirm that the inhibition of ParB condensation by the free CTD occurs without displacement of full length ParB from DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The free CTD of ParB blocks the formation of ParB networks via a dominant negative effect on a key protein-protein bridging interface.
source: Our data indicates that the free CTD of ParB blocks the formation of ParB networks via a dominant negative effect on a key protein-protein bridging interface.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Single ~24 kbps DNA molecules lacking the parS sequence were laterally stretched using a home-built magnet holder.
source: We laterally stretched single ~24 kbps DNA molecules lacking the parS sequence (see Materials and methods) (Figure 2A) using a home-built magnet holder that can pull DNA molecules from one side (Madariaga-Marcos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the experiments performed.

claim: The lateral magnet device can apply forces of ~1 pN on 1 μm beads.
source: This device can apply forces of ~1 pN on 1 μm beads, which is sufficient to prevent condensation of DNA upon introduction of ParB.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the device used.

claim: A force of ~1 pN is sufficient to prevent condensation of DNA upon introduction of ParB.
source: This device can apply forces of ~1 pN on 1 μm beads, which is sufficient to prevent condensation of DNA upon introduction of ParB.
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the force required to prevent condensation.

claim: ParB2S68C-AlexaFluor488 (ParB2AF) retained wild-type DNA-binding properties in bulk assays.
source: We produced a fluorescent variant of ParB labelled with Alexa Fluor 488 (ParB2S68C-AlexaFluor488, hereafter ParB2AF), which retained wild-type DNA-binding properties in our established bulk assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental validation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injection of ParB2AF in the flow cell resulted in a gradual increase of fluorescence concomitant to the arrival and non-specific binding of the protein to the DNA.
source: Injection of the protein in the flow cell resulted in a gradual increase of fluorescence concomitant to the arrival and non-specific binding of the protein to the DNA (Video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 1.

claim: Sometimes a fraction of the DNA closer to the magnetic bead remained invisible in the fluorescence signal.
source: Note, however, that sometimes a fraction of the DNA closer to the magnetic bead remained invisible in the fluorescence signal (Video 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 2.

claim: The invisibility of DNA near the bead is due to the limited penetration of the excitation light produced by TIRF, the tilting angle of the DNA (≤5⁰), the attachment point of the DNA at the bead, and the fixed bead orientation under the magnetic field.
source: This is as expected and is due to the limited penetration of the excitation light produced by TIRF, the tilting angle of the DNA (≤5⁰), the attachment point of the DNA at the bead, and the fixed bead orientation under the magnetic field.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the technical properties of the TIRF setup.

claim: The integrated intensity in the area of a DNA molecule remained constant for the longest time points tested (2 min) in the absence of an oxygen scavenger system.
source: The integrated intensity in the area of a DNA molecule remained constant for the longest time points tested (2 min) in the absence of an oxygen scavenger system, suggesting a continuous and fast exchange of ParB proteins with the surrounding media (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The constant integrated intensity suggests a continuous and fast exchange of ParB proteins with the surrounding media.
source: The integrated intensity in the area of a DNA molecule remained constant for the longest time points tested (2 min) in the absence of an oxygen scavenger system, suggesting a continuous and fast exchange of ParB proteins with the surrounding media (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The integrated intensity differs between molecules due to the fraction of DNA imaged, which depends on the anchoring point of the DNA on the bead.
source: The integrated intensity differs between molecules due to the fraction of DNA imaged, which depends on the anchoring point of the DNA on the bead.
evidence: This is an explanation for the variability in intensity measurements.

claim: Kymographs taken along the DNA showed variations in fluorescence intensity with time, confirming continuous and fast exchange.
source: This was further confirmed in kymographs taken along the DNA that showed variations in fluorescence intensity with time (Figure 2D, Video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: A gradual decrease of fluorescence intensity was observed when the protein was removed from free solution by flowing buffer alone.
source: As expected, we did observe a gradual decrease of fluorescence intensity when the protein was removed from free solution by flowing buffer alone (Video 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Control experiments crosslinking ParB with formaldehyde indicated a photobleaching half-life time for Alexa Fluor of around 28 s.
source: Control experiments crosslinking ParB with formaldehyde indicated a photobleaching half-life time for Alexa Fluor of around 28 s, much shorter than the duration of our measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The photobleaching half-life time of Alexa Fluor (28 s) is much shorter than the duration of the measurements.
source: Control experiments crosslinking ParB with formaldehyde indicated a photobleaching half-life time for Alexa Fluor of around 28 s, much shorter than the duration of our measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a comparison between the photobleaching time and measurement duration.

claim: The rapid exchange of the protein was confirmed in fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments.
source: The rapid exchange of the protein was further confirmed in fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments. They consisted of photo-bleaching all ParBAF molecules included in the visualisation area inside the TIRF field by using a high-laser power pulse, and then monitoring the fluorescence recovery of the protein-DNA complex in the presence of 250 nM ParBAF (Video 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Video 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The experiments demonstrate the dynamic interaction of ParB with DNA under forces that are non-permissive for condensation.
source: Altogether, these experiments demonstrate the dynamic interaction of ParB with DNA under forces that are non-permissive for condensation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The arrival of the protein at the site of interest in single-channel flow cells is gradual, typically requires tens of seconds to reach equilibrium, and it is difficult to assign arrival times.
source: However, the arrival of the protein at the site of interest in single-channel flow cells is gradual, typically requires tens of seconds to reach equilibrium, and it is difficult to assign arrival times (Gollnick et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a known limitation of single-channel flow cells cited from Gollnick et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Flowing at high rates increases the force applied on the DNA as a result of the drag force on the bead and can lead to structural distortions of the DNA duplex.
source: Moreover, flowing at high rates increases the force applied on the DNA as a result of the drag force on the bead and can lead to structural distortions of the DNA duplex, ultimately interfering with protein binding (Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a known effect of high flow rates cited from Xiao et al., 2011.

claim: A fast buffer exchange system based on multilaminar flow cells was developed to reduce reagent exchange times and the contribution of the flow on the total force on the DNA.
source: In order to reduce reagent exchange times and the contribution of the flow on the total force on the DNA, we developed a fast buffer exchange system based on multilaminar flow cells (Liu et al., 2013) (Tan et al., 2007) (Brouwer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological development described in the manuscript.

claim: Flow cells with two inlets were used, where two reagents are introduced (i.e. protein and buffer), and a single outlet.
source: We used flow cells with two inlets, where two reagents are introduced (i.e. protein and buffer), and a single outlet (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the flow cell design shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dimensions of the flow cells and the flow rates used (≤500 µl/min) ensure a laminar flow regime under which the two reagents do not significantly mix.
source: The dimensions of our flow cells and the flow rates we used (≤500 µl/min) ensure a laminar flow regime under which the two reagents do not significantly mix (Materials and methods) (Brewer and Bianco, 2008).
evidence: This is a technical property of the flow cell system cited from Brewer and Bianco, 2008.

claim: Fast alternation between buffer and protein was achieved by varying the flow rates of the syringes (190 µl/min and 10 µl/min) and maintaining a constant flow rate in the central channel (200 µl/min).
source: Fast alternation between buffer and protein was achieved by varying the flow rates of the syringes (190 µl/min and 10 µl/min) and maintaining a constant flow rate in the central channel (200 µl/min).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the flow system.

claim: The multilaminar flow system reduced reagent switching times and allowed assignment of reagents arrival times while keeping a low total force (~3.5 pN) on the DNA.
source: This reduced reagent switching times, and allowed us to assign reagents arrival times while keeping a low total force (~3.5 pN) on the DNA (Materials and methods) which is non-permissive for condensation by ParB.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the multilaminar flow system.

claim: A force of ~3.5 pN is non-permissive for condensation by ParB.
source: This reduced reagent switching times, and allowed us to assign reagents arrival times while keeping a low total force (~3.5 pN) on the DNA (Materials and methods) which is non-permissive for condensation by ParB.
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the force required to prevent condensation.

claim: Protein concentrations could be accurately controlled as the DNA was exposed within a few seconds to the condition of interest.
source: Furthermore, protein concentrations could be accurately controlled as the DNA was exposed within a few seconds (see below) to the condition of interest, allowing one to measure association and dissociation constants.
evidence: This is a capability of the multilaminar flow system.

claim: The boundary achieves a complete shifting in ~6.5 s.
source: Our results concluded that the boundary achieves a complete shifting in ~6.5 s.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the boundary shifting time.

claim: The fluorescence intensity decreased when buffer was flowed and it was recovered by the introduction of ParBAF.
source: The fluorescence intensity decreased when buffer was flowed (shadowed area) and it was recovered by the introduction of ParBAF.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the laminar flow experiments.

claim: The binding curve of ParBAF on the DNA was readily different from that of the background despite the limitation of fluid exchange kinetics.
source: Note that despite the limitation of fluid exchange kinetics, the binding curve of ParBAF on the DNA was readily different from that of the background.
evidence: This is an experimental observation indicating the sensitivity of the assay.

claim: The lower k_off in wild type ParB compared to ParBR82A might reflect localised condensation events in the wild type protein.
source: This might reflect localised condensation events in the wild type protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the difference in k_off values.

claim: At high ParB concentrations (≥500 nM), ParB-ParB interactions are favored likely resulting in local condensates, which prevent unbinding of the protein.
source: This is particularly relevant at the high concentrations used (≥500 nM), where ParB-ParB interactions are favored likely resulting in local condensates, which prevent unbinding of the protein.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavior at high concentrations.

claim: The saturation in k_obs cannot be explained by limitations in the temporal resolution of the assay (acquisition rate ~10 s−1).
source: This cannot be explained by limitations in the temporal resolution of our assay (acquisition rate ~10 s−1) and we therefore favour the idea that it is limited by our fluid exchange kinetics.
evidence: This is an interpretation ruling out one possible explanation.

claim: The saturation in k_obs is likely limited by fluid exchange kinetics.
source: This cannot be explained by limitations in the temporal resolution of our assay (acquisition rate ~10 s−1) and we therefore favour the idea that it is limited by our fluid exchange kinetics.
evidence: This is a favored interpretation of the saturation effect.

claim: The saturation in k_obs can also be explained by rate limiting events after the formation of a collision complex.
source: Nevertheless, the saturation observed can also be explained by rate limiting events after the formation of a collision complex (which are not considered in our simple model).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the saturation effect.

claim: The estimated k_on (~4 x 10^5 M−1 s−1) was one order of magnitude below a published value for a mutant ParB (~2.1 x 10^6 M−1 s−1).
source: Our estimation (~4 x 105 M−1 s−1) was one order of magnitude below a published value for a mutant ParB, ~2.1 x 106 M−1 s−1 (Song et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a comparison to a previously reported value cited from Song et al., 2016.

claim: The discrepancy in k_on may reflect a different binding mechanism of the wild-type ParB protein compared to the condensation-defective mutant.
source: This discrepancy may reflect a different binding mechanism of the wild-type ParB protein employed here compared to the condensation-defective mutant, and/or simply the limitations of our laminar-flow-based technology.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the discrepancy in k_on values.

claim: The discrepancy in k_on may be due to the limitations of the laminar-flow-based technology.
source: This discrepancy may reflect a different binding mechanism of the wild-type ParB protein employed here compared to the condensation-defective mutant, and/or simply the limitations of our laminar-flow-based technology.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the discrepancy in k_on values.

claim: Previous work indicated distinct DNA-binding mechanisms for ParB in the presence of Mg2+ or EDTA.
source: Our previous work indicated distinct DNA-binding mechanisms for ParB in the presence of Mg2+ or EDTA (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Taylor et al., 2015.

claim: The specific binding of ParB was only observed in Mg2+.
source: In particular, the specific binding of the protein was only observed in Mg2+, while the non-specific binding was promoted by the presence of EDTA, especially at low ParB concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work about ParB binding mechanisms.

claim: The non-specific binding of ParB was promoted by the presence of EDTA, especially at low ParB concentrations.
source: In particular, the specific binding of the protein was only observed in Mg2+, while the non-specific binding was promoted by the presence of EDTA, especially at low ParB concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work about ParB binding mechanisms.

claim: The presence of EDTA strengthens interactions between ParB and non-specific DNA.
source: In summary, and in agreement with our published observations (Fisher et al., 2017), we conclude that the presence of EDTA strengthens interactions between ParB and non-specific DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and agreement with previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: CTDAF complexes were observed at high CTDAF concentrations (10 μM) in the presence of EDTA.
source: We observed protein:DNA complexes at high CTDAF concentrations (10 μM) in the presence of EDTA but no complexes were visible in the presence of a magnesium-containing buffer at the same concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No CTDAF:DNA complexes were visible in the presence of a magnesium-containing buffer at 10 μM CTDAF concentration.
source: We observed protein:DNA complexes at high CTDAF concentrations (10 μM) in the presence of EDTA but no complexes were visible in the presence of a magnesium-containing buffer at the same concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of CTDAF complexes remained constant over time, suggesting continuous and rapid exchange between bound and free CTD proteins.
source: The fluorescence intensity of CTDAF complexes remained constant over time, suggesting continuous and rapid exchange between bound and free CTD proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 6).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 6.

claim: The CTD of ParB can bind and unbind rapidly from DNA, but only under EDTA conditions.
source: Altogether, these results show that the CTD of ParB can bind and unbind rapidly from DNA, but only under EDTA conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The free CTD will not inhibit the interactions of full length ParB with DNA by simple competition under Mg2+ conditions.
source: This implies that the free CTD will not inhibit the interactions of full length ParB with DNA by simple competition under Mg2+ conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that CTD only binds DNA in EDTA conditions.

claim: The CTD can compete for DNA but only under EDTA conditions.
source: Therefore, as expected based on the properties of the free CTD alone, it can compete for DNA but only under EDTA conditions, which are not considered to have any particular biological relevance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: EDTA conditions are not considered to have any particular biological relevance.
source: Therefore, as expected based on the properties of the free CTD alone, it can compete for DNA but only under EDTA conditions, which are not considered to have any particular biological relevance.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological relevance of the experimental conditions.

claim: Scenarios 1 and 2 can be discounted because the CTD does not reduce DNA binding by full length ParB under Mg2+ conditions.
source: These results strongly suggest that scenarios 1 and 2 (Figure 1) can be discounted, because the CTD does not reduce DNA binding by full length ParB under Mg2+ conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data ruling out two proposed mechanisms.

claim: Previous experiments showed that an excess of the CTD of ParB prevents the condensation of DNA tethers.
source: Previous experiments showed that an excess of the CTD of ParB prevents the condensation of DNA tethers and also promotes decondensation of preformed ParB-DNA networks (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: Previous experiments showed that an excess of the CTD of ParB promotes decondensation of preformed ParB-DNA networks.
source: Previous experiments showed that an excess of the CTD of ParB prevents the condensation of DNA tethers and also promotes decondensation of preformed ParB-DNA networks (Fisher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work cited as Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: Condensation events were initiated by ParBAF by reducing the force from 1 to 0.2 pN and were directly visualised by fluorescence microscopy in laterally stretched DNA molecules.
source: Condensation events were initiated by ParBAF by reducing the force from 1 to 0.2 pN and were directly visualised by fluorescence microscopy in laterally stretched DNA molecules (Figure 5A, Video 7).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A and Video 7.

claim: The condensation process could be stopped by increasing the force.
